description: Care settings, the five rights of service users, and what those rights look like in practice.
content_html:
What Are Health and Social Care Settings?

Health and social care settings are the places where people go to receive care, treatment or support. They range from a busy NHS hospital ward to a small community centre running a drop-in session for older adults. Understanding where care takes place is the first step in understanding how rights and values apply in practice.

Health care settings include dental practices, GP surgeries, health centres, hospitals, nursing homes, opticians, pharmacies and walk-in centres. In a dental practice, for example, a dental nurse treats patients with toothache, carries out check-ups and provides oral health advice. In a walk-in centre, a triage nurse assesses people who cannot get a same-day GP appointment.

Social care settings include community centres, day centres, foodbanks, homeless shelters, residential homes, retirement homes, social services departments and support groups. A residential home for older adults, for instance, provides 24-hour personal care for residents who can no longer manage at home. A community centre may run a dementia café every Thursday morning, supporting carers and service users together.

Key Fact

There are eight health care settings (dental practice, GP surgery, health centre, hospital, nursing home, opticians, pharmacy, walk-in centre) and eight social care settings (community centre, day centre, foodbank, homeless shelter, residential home, retirement home, social services department, support group). The distinction matters: health settings focus on clinical care; social care settings focus on personal and practical support.

The Five Rights of Service Users

Every person who uses a health or social care setting is entitled to five key rights. These are not optional extras — service providers are expected to uphold them at all times. Failing to respect these rights can harm the service user’s physical and emotional wellbeing and may constitute professional misconduct.

Right to Choice

The right to choice means service users can make decisions about their own care. In a 30-bed nursing home, this might mean a resident choosing what to wear each morning, selecting from a menu at meal times, or deciding whether to attend a group activity session. A key worker who overrides a service user’s preferences — for example, dressing them in clothes they have not chosen — is failing to respect this right. Choice is the foundation of a person feeling in control of their own life.

Right to Confidentiality

The right to confidentiality means personal information is shared only on a need-to-know basis. At a GP surgery, a patient’s medical record is not shared with reception staff who do not need it, and certainly not with family members without the patient’s consent. Confidentiality builds trust: service users are more likely to disclose sensitive health information if they know it will be handled carefully. It is important to understand, however, that confidentiality is not absolute — where there is a serious safeguarding concern, the duty to protect someone from harm may override the duty to keep information confidential.

Right to Consultation

The right to consultation means service users are included in planning and reviewing their own care. In a community mental health team, this might mean a care coordinator discussing a service user’s support plan with them before any changes are made, rather than presenting a done deal. Consultation respects the service user as the expert on their own experience and produces care plans that are more likely to be followed.

Right to Equal and Fair Treatment

The right to equal and fair treatment means every service user receives the same standard of care regardless of their age, disability, gender, race, religion or any other characteristic. In a hospital ward, a patient with a learning disability should receive the same quality of pain management as any other patient. Practitioners must not make assumptions about a service user’s preferences, intelligence or wishes based on stereotypes. Equal treatment does not mean identical treatment — it means each person’s individual needs are met without discrimination.

Right to Protection from Abuse and Harm

The right to protection from abuse and harm requires care settings to take active steps to keep service users safe. This includes having staff who are properly trained, DBS-checked and supervised, and having clear procedures for raising concerns. At an after-school club for primary-aged children, this right is upheld by conducting thorough staff recruitment checks, ensuring adult-to-child ratios are maintained, and having a clear policy for reporting a concern about a child’s welfare.

Key Fact

The five rights are: choice (making your own decisions), confidentiality (personal information kept private), consultation (being involved in planning your care), equal and fair treatment (no discrimination) and protection from abuse and harm (kept safe by trained, checked staff). Every service user in every setting is entitled to all five.

Students often mix up rights and person-centred values in exam answers, costing marks. Rights (Topic Area 1) are entitlements that service users have in any care setting — they exist whether or not a practitioner remembers them. Person-centred values (Topic Area 2) are principles that practitioners apply when delivering care — things like dignity, respect and individuality. The two concepts interlock, but they are tested separately. A service user’s right to choice is distinct from the practitioner’s value of encouraging decision making. The right is the entitlement; the value describes how a practitioner behaves to honour it.

A common error in exam answers is to write that “information must never be shared” when discussing confidentiality. In fact, confidentiality is a right with limits. If a service user discloses information suggesting that they, or someone else, is at serious risk of abuse or harm, the practitioner has a duty to pass that information to the appropriate person — for example, the Designated Safeguarding Lead. The right to confidentiality and the right to protection from abuse sit alongside each other: safeguarding disclosure can and does override confidentiality. Examiners reward answers that acknowledge this nuance.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark ‘Describe’ question about rights in a named setting, the most common mistake is describing the right in general terms without anchoring it to the specific scenario. For example, if the question names a residential care home and asks you to describe how two rights are upheld, you must link each right to a feature of that setting — not write a generic definition. Write two sentences per right: one naming the right and one explaining what it looks like in that particular setting. The command word ‘Describe’ (OCR definition: “give an account including all the relevant characteristics, qualities or events”) requires more than a label — it requires detail that is grounded in the named context.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health care settings (GP surgery, hospital, dental practice, etc.) and social care settings (residential home, community centre, etc.) are the environments where service users receive care — and all five rights apply in both types.
  • The five rights are choice, confidentiality, consultation, equal and fair treatment, and protection from abuse and harm — every service user is entitled to all five in every setting.
  • Rights and person-centred values are related but distinct: rights are entitlements service users have; values are principles practitioners apply. Confidentiality is not absolute — safeguarding concerns override it.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a social care setting?
A) GP surgery
B) Walk-in centre
C) Residential home
D) Hospital
Name one health care setting and one social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one health care setting (e.g. dental practice, GP surgery, hospital, nursing home, opticians, pharmacy, walk-in centre, health centre) AND one social care setting (e.g. residential home, community centre, foodbank, day centre, retirement home, homeless shelter, social services department, support group). Both must be correctly categorised to earn the mark.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the right to consultation in a health or social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that service users are involved in decisions about their own care; 1 mark for a brief qualifying detail (e.g. care plans are discussed with the service user before changes are made; the service user's views are sought and considered).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a GP surgery could uphold two of the five rights of its service users.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per right described. Accept any two rights with relevant application to a GP surgery setting. Example responses: Right to confidentiality (2 marks) -- 1 mark for identifying the right; 1 mark for a specific feature of a GP surgery (e.g. patient medical records are stored securely and only shared with clinicians who need them; a receptionist does not discuss a patient's appointment reason in a crowded waiting area). Right to choice (2 marks) -- 1 mark for identifying the right; 1 mark for a specific feature (e.g. a patient chooses between two treatment options discussed with their GP; a patient selects a preferred appointment time). Other rights awarded on the same principle: consultation, equal and fair treatment, or protection from abuse and harm, each with a GP surgery-specific example.

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important for service users in a residential care home to have their right to choice upheld.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the right to choice (e.g. residents can make decisions about their own care and daily life); 1 mark for a reason using 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that' (e.g. because it means they feel in control of their own lives); 1 mark for a further developed reason or consequence (e.g. therefore their emotional wellbeing is supported and they are less likely to feel powerless or lose their sense of identity).

practice_questions.text:
Fatima is a Healthcare Assistant on a 20-bed elderly care ward in an NHS hospital. One of her service users is Mr Okeke, a 78-year-old man who has recently been admitted following a fall. Mr Okeke speaks limited English and has a visual impairment.

Explain how the ward team could uphold three of the five rights for Mr Okeke during his stay. In your answer, refer to his specific circumstances.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies three rights clearly and links each to Mr Okeke's specific circumstances (limited English, visual impairment, hospital setting). Uses correct terminology throughout. Provides a clear chain of reasoning for each right using language such as 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that'. Example content -- right to consultation: the ward team should involve Mr Okeke in decisions about his treatment and discharge plan, therefore he feels respected and his care is tailored to his needs, even if this requires extra time or an interpreter. Right to equal and fair treatment: Mr Okeke must receive the same standard of pain management and clinical care as any other patient, because his language difference and visual impairment should not lead to assumptions about his preferences or capacity. Right to confidentiality: his medical information should not be shared with family members without his consent, even if they visit, because this respects his autonomy and builds trust with the care team.

Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies at least two rights with generally accurate explanation and some application to Mr Okeke, but may lack development or miss one of his specific circumstances.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies rights correctly but explanation is descriptive rather than reasoned; limited reference to Mr Okeke's circumstances.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a right with little or no explanation or application to the scenario.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a health care setting?
Which of the five rights means a service user can make their own decisions about their care and daily life?
options: Right to equal and fair treatment

knowledge_checks.q: The right to _____ means a service user's personal information is shared only with those who need it to provide care.
The right to _____ means service users are involved in decisions about planning and reviewing their own care.
Match each right to the correct description:
left: Right to equal and fair treatment
Right to protection from abuse and harm
right: Service users make decisions about their own care and daily life
Every service user receives the same standard of care regardless of their background
Care settings take active steps to keep service users safe through training and procedures

flashcard_questions.q: What is a health care setting?
flashcard_questions.a: An environment where people receive medical treatment, clinical examination or health monitoring.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a social care setting?
flashcard_questions.a: An environment where people receive personal care, support or practical help to live safely or independently.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four examples of health care settings.
flashcard_questions.a: Any four of: dental practice, GP surgery, hospital, nursing home, opticians, pharmacy, walk-in centre, health centre.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four examples of social care settings.
flashcard_questions.a: Any four of: residential home, community centre, day centre, foodbank, homeless shelter, retirement home, social services department, support group.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the right to choice for a service user?
flashcard_questions.a: The entitlement to make their own decisions about their care, treatment and daily life.

flashcard_questions.q: Name any two of the five rights of service users.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: choice, confidentiality, consultation, equal and fair treatment, protection from abuse and harm.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the right to choice mean for a service user?
flashcard_questions.a: The right to make their own decisions about their care, treatment and daily life.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the right to confidentiality protect?
flashcard_questions.a: Personal information, shared only with those who need it to provide care.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the right to consultation mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Service users are involved in planning and reviewing decisions about their own care.

flashcard_questions.q: What does equal and fair treatment mean in a care setting?
flashcard_questions.a: Every service user receives the same standard of care regardless of age, disability, gender, race or religion.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a residential home uphold the right to protection from abuse and harm?
flashcard_questions.a: By employing DBS-checked, trained staff and having clear procedures for reporting concerns.

flashcard_questions.q: Is confidentiality always absolute in a care setting?
flashcard_questions.a: No. A safeguarding concern about serious risk of harm can override the duty of confidentiality.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between rights and person-centred values?
flashcard_questions.a: Rights are entitlements service users have; person-centred values are principles practitioners apply when delivering care.

glossary_terms.definition: An environment where people receive clinical treatment or health monitoring, such as a GP surgery, hospital or dental practice.
An environment where people receive personal care, practical support or emotional assistance, such as a residential home or community centre.
A person who uses a health or social care service, such as a patient, resident or client.
The entitlement of a service user to make their own decisions about their care, treatment and daily life.
The entitlement of a service user to have their personal information kept private and only shared with those who need it to deliver care.
The entitlement of a service user to be involved in planning and reviewing decisions about their own care and treatment.

glossary_terms.term: right to equal and fair treatment
glossary_terms.definition: The entitlement of a service user to receive the same standard of care as anyone else, free from discrimination.

glossary_terms.term: right to protection from abuse and harm
glossary_terms.definition: The entitlement of a service user to be kept safe through trained, DBS-checked staff and clear safeguarding procedures.
